summary: Time protocols such as NTP and NTS keep several IANA registries of assigned values. Some entries were wrong or did not follow normal practice. This RFC reviews all of the NTP and NTS registries and corrects them so they are accurate and consistent.

eli5.summary: Imagine a phone book with a few wrong numbers and odd entries. This is the clean-up that checks every page and fixes the mistakes in the lists for clock-setting protocols.

subtitle: A clean-up of the IANA registries for NTP and NTS, fixing wrong entries and setting common rules.

tldr.problem: Some of the NTP and NTS registries contain incorrect assignments or do not follow common practice, such as swapped nibbles in extension field types.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9748 reviews every NTP and NTS registry, switches the policy to Specification Required, reserves experimental ranges, and replaces the Extension Field Types table.
tldr.outcome: The registries are now consistent and documented, and RFC 9748 updates RFCs 5905, 5906, 7821, 7822 and 8573.

today: RFC 9748 is a Proposed Standard and no RFC obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 5905, RFC 5906, RFC 7821, RFC 7822 and RFC 8573.

sections.title: Why the Registries Needed a Review
sections.content:
The Network Time Protocol (NTP) and Network Time Security (NTS) documents define a number of registries, collectively called the NTP registries. Some are correct, but some include incorrect assignments and some do not follow common practice. This document reviews all of them for completeness and corrects them where necessary.

The bulk of the document has two parts: a summary of the relevant registries, with syntax requirements, registration procedures and defining documents, and a revised format and entries for each registry being modified. It does not describe how an implementation processes the fields.
sections.eli5: Someone checked every list used by the clock-setting protocols and fixed the ones with mistakes.

sections.title: The Existing Registries
sections.content:
RFC 5905 defines two registries: "NTP Reference Identifier Codes" and "NTP Kiss-o'-Death Codes". Both hold codes of up to four ASCII characters, padded on the right with all-bits-zero. Entries starting with 0x58, the ASCII letter uppercase X, are reserved for Private or Experimental Use. Both were First Come First Served.

The "NTP Extension Field Types" registry is the messy one. RFC 5905 defines the on-the-wire format of extension fields without creating a registry. RFC 5906 mentions the registry and defines it indirectly through 30 extensions (10 each for request, response and error response). RFC 7821 adds a Checksum Complement entry and RFC 8915 adds four entries.

The RFC lists two problems. Many entries have swapped nibbles; for example 0x0302 was listed for Cookie Message Request instead of 0x0203, because of documentation errors in the original Autokey implementation. Some values were also mistakenly reused. The NTS registries from RFC 8915 are listed for completeness, with no changes.
sections.eli5: Some labels in the list had their digits swapped by accident, and a few labels were handed out twice.

sections.title: The New Rules
sections.content:
Three general guidelines apply. A partition of the Extension Field Types registry is reserved for Private or Experimental Use. In the Reference Identifier and Kiss-o'-Death registries, ASCII entries are now limited to uppercase letters or digits, and fields starting with uppercase "X" (0x58) are reserved for Private or Experimental Use. The policy for each registry is now Specification Required, as defined in Section 4.6 of RFC 8126.

Both the Reference Identifier and Kiss-o'-Death registries get new Notes saying codes beginning with "X" are reserved for experimentation and development and IANA cannot assign them. Existing entries are left unchanged. The columns are an ID (four bytes, padded on the right with all-bits-zero), a description, and the defining reference.
sections.eli5: New rules say names must use capital letters and digits, anything starting with X is for experiments, and a written description must exist before a name is handed out.

sections.title: The Extension Field Types Table
sections.content:
The Extension Field Types registry now has Specification Required, with RFC 5906 and this document added as references. Field Types from 0xF000 through 0xFFFF are reserved for experimentation and development and IANA cannot assign them. The columns are Field Type (a two-byte hexadecimal value), Meaning and Reference.

The erroneous swapped-nibble values, such as 0x0002, 0x0302 and 0x8902, are marked "Reserved for historic reasons". They are reserved rather than deleted in case some implementation used the registered values instead of what the original Autokey implementation used. A Note also says that NTS Cookie and Autokey Message Request share the Field Type 0x0204; in practice this is not a problem because other parts of the message determine the field semantics.

Each entry in Section 4 is intended to completely replace the existing entry with the same name.
sections.eli5: The wrong labels were not thrown away. They were put on hold with a note saying why, in case someone was already using them.

sections.title: Designated Experts and Security
sections.content:
The IESG is asked to choose three designated experts (DEs), and approvals from two are required to implement a change. DEs should be familiar with RFC 8126, check that a suitable specification exists and is publicly available, and check the clarity of purpose and use of requested code points. They should also know this document, including the history it records.

The Security Considerations say the document adds no new security considerations, since those are defined in the document that defines each extension; see the References column of the relevant IANA registry.
sections.eli5: A small panel of three experts checks new requests, and two of them must agree before anything changes.
